title: Purpose and what RichView maximizes
summary:
This part settles what RichView is for before anything is rebuilt: the definition, positioning and audience, the core jobs, one reference journey and the flagship, what RichView maximizes and in which order, the bets meant to go beyond existing tools, explicit non-goals, which members of the product family the rewrite builds, licence and source visibility, public presence, distribution and launch, domains and hosting, what carries over from today’s code, the corrections that must never recur, and how the rewrite and the product are judged.

The answers that shape everything else: the definition (INT-01) and audience (INT-06); the order of maximization targets (INT-17), with safety as a floor (INT-79) and traceability and editability as guarantees rather than ranked targets (INT-11); what the rewrite builds (INT-31, with Cowork in INT-83, Publish in INT-35, News in INT-74, the sharing model in INT-36 and managed hosting in INT-27); licence, source visibility and distribution (INT-37, INT-38, INT-71), which together decide whether anyone can install RichView at launch; and what “rewrite” means for existing code (INT-49).

Answer each card: **accept** keeps the proposal as written (where options are listed, the proposal is the recommendation); **edit** replaces it with your text; **reject** drops it from the rewrite; **defer** leaves it open. On non-goal cards (INT-24 to INT-30, INT-80), reject lifts the exclusion; it does not build the feature. On rule cards (INT-56 to INT-66), reject means the rule does not bind agents. INT-67 counts only product items towards done; one-off outward actions such as archiving, redirects and shutdowns are tracked in part 08. Part 08's cross-part contradiction cards (OPN-50 to OPN-68) decide conflicts involving this part's cards and should be answered first.

Decisions here carry `D-` IDs, and the standing rules (INT-56 to INT-66) carry `G-` IDs that part 02 references for its gates instead of defining its own; every ID is unique across parts. Three delivery corrections are owned by part 02 rather than repeated here: production deploys only from `prod` (G-DEPLOY-OWNER, DEL-40); parallel agents work in isolated worktrees with recorded provenance; and every task starts from fresh `dev`, never a stale checkout (G-WORKTREE-ISOLATION, DEL-42; OPN-30). Delivery mechanics and gates are in part 02, components in 03, features in 04, types in 05, styles in 06, budgets in 07, and open PRs and one-off actions in 08; cards here point there instead of repeating them. Repository sources are pinned to `b4db233` and dated by the commit that last changed the cited line; live checks are dated 2026-10-21 or 2026-10-22.

items.title: Why RichView: three value claims
items.question: Are the three reasons on the live page RichView’s value claims, which the rewrite must visibly prove?
items.why: Each claim commits the product to something testable: a reusable design system, a plain-text handoff that travels with its render, and a fit with editors and Git.
items.proposed: RichView makes three value claims. **Keep design consistent:** typography, chart conventions and styles are reusable decisions, made once and applied to every analysis. **Make the handoff inspectable:** words, chart definitions and data are plain text, and the rendered page travels with its source. **Stay in the workflow you know:** write with your agent, revise in your editor and version the report beside its evidence in Git. The renderer owns charts, layout and typography so the agent can concentrate on the analysis.

items.title: The artifact: plain-text source, self-contained output
items.question: Is a report’s main output one self-contained HTML file that opens offline, rather than a page that links a shared runtime and fonts?
items.why: It decides whether reports embed their runtime and fonts (portable, heavy) or link shared assets (light, tied to a host), and what sharing a story means.
items.proposed: A report’s main output is one self-contained HTML file: it embeds its runtime and fonts and opens from disk, offline and without a server. items.title: What RichView is chosen over
items.question: Which alternatives does RichView position itself against, and why would an author choose it over each?
items.why: Part 01 defines RichView but never names what it replaces. The June research built the wedge on four alternatives; naming them fixes which comparisons the site, docs and posts make and which ones the product must win.
items.proposed: RichView is chosen over four alternatives, each for one reason. Over screenshotting a plotted chart and eyeballing it: exact, machine-readable defects at no cost per render. Over raw chart libraries: reference-grade charts from the defaults, with no per-chart tuning, and charts that check themselves. Over chat artifacts and code interpreters: a durable, sourced report the author keeps and versions, not an ephemeral blob. Over BI tools and notebooks: no infrastructure, one file, and checks at the rendering layer rather than only the data layer. Public pages describe these as categories, not named products (INT-23).

items.title: Secondary audience: readers of the stories
items.question: What must a reader of a RichView story get, on which devices, without installing anything?
items.why: Readers never see the source. This sets the reading floor every component must meet on phones, desktops, print and assistive technology.
items.proposed: Readers open a story on a phone, a desktop or as a PDF with nothing to install, and with no account unless its author shared it only with signed-in readers, such as their organization on RichView Cowork (OPN-54, INT-83). Every story reads completely from 320 px wide upward, works with a keyboard, gives charts and controls accessible names, honours reduced motion, and keeps text and tables legible with scripts disabled. Charts render with WebGL (INT-31) and must work in recent Safari, Firefox and Chrome; where JavaScript or WebGL is unavailable, each chart's frame keeps its title, caption and source note and shows a notice that the chart cannot be displayed, with no snapshot, image or table in its place (ARC-05). Readers can reach each chart’s values, at the precision the author chose (FEA-CH-37), and its sources. People who meet RichView through shared stories or posts are readers first. The stories come mostly from analysts and also from other writers, such as journalists and people running their own RichView site or blog (INT-06).

items.title: Core jobs
items.question: Which jobs does RichView do for its authors?
items.why: The jobs bound the feature parts (04): a feature that serves none of them is out of the rewrite.
items.proposed: RichView does five jobs. **Write:** the agent turns finished analysis into Rich Markdown with chart-local data, guided by `richview learn` and the skill. **Check:** validation and chart diagnostics tell the agent, in machine-readable form, what is broken or unreadable. **Present:** one source renders into a typeset, interactive story in any accepted style. **Revise:** the human reviews the rendered story beside its source in the editor or browser, and the agent fixes it. **Share:** the story leaves as a self-contained file, a PDF or a stable versioned URL. RichView does not run the analysis or query data sources; the agent brings the data.

items.question: Which single end-to-end journey is the reference scenario for the guide and the acceptance tests?
items.why: A named journey makes the jobs testable: the rewrite is not usable until this path works without workarounds.
items.proposed: An analyst asks their agent for a weekly sales story. The agent runs `richview learn`, creates `reports/weekly-sales/report.rmd` with prose, three charts and a table that read chart-local CSV files, and renders it through `richview_render`. `richview_check` reports a dropped label; the agent shortens it and the check comes back clean. The analyst previews in VS Code, switches style, asks for a sharper headline and exports a PDF. The agent publishes version 0.1.0 to the team’s server and commits source and data to Git. A colleague opens the link on a phone; shared in a chat, the link unfurls as a card with the story’s thumbnail (INT-07). Every step except publishing and the link preview works offline.

items.title: Storytelling
items.question: Does RichView maximize how clearly a story argues, not only how it looks?
items.why: RichView sells data stories, and the design-and-hosting brief pairs motion with “strong storytelling”, but no target covered narrative quality, so INT-17 could not rank it.
items.proposed: RichView maximizes storytelling: a story leads with its claims and carries the reader through the evidence. items.title: Single-author core; one hosted service for data and media
items.question: Does RichView's core stay single-author and free of accounts, with roles only on self-hosted RichView servers, and is managed hosting for large data and media the one service RichView itself operates?
items.why: Accounts, tenants, billing, comments and co-editing each turn a renderer into an operated service with security, privacy and support duties. Daniel's INT-06 answer puts roles and approvals on RichView's servers and never in the core, and his INT-31 answer has RichView run managed hosting for large data and media as a service, which ends the earlier rule that RichView operates none. This card draws both lines.
items.proposed:
RichView's core, the format, renderer, CLI, MCP server and VS Code extension, is single-author: it has no user accounts, roles or approvals, and review happens in Git and in the author's tools. Self-hosted RichView servers have a basic role set: reader, author and owner, with rights to edit, delete and share. They are RichView Publish (external-facing, INT-35) and RichView Cowork (internal-facing, INT-83), which share one server core; a writer's own small server for a personal site or blog is one of the two (INT-83), and whoever runs a server operates its accounts. Approvals, where a server has them, decide what gets published, as Publish's editorial workflow does (INT-22). In the browser a server offers only that approval, a yes or no on the pending change, and an author's quick source edit, never a full editor (INT-26).

RichView itself operates one service for others: managed hosting for large data and media that reports reference through pinned asset references (TYP-41), uploaded with `richview asset` and the MCP asset tools (FEA-SF-50, ARC-34); authors may host the same assets themselves instead. RichView hosts no reports for others: no RichView-run Cowork or Publish tenancy, comment threads, real-time co-editing or template marketplace (INT-36); the one Publish instance it runs is its own News (INT-74). The hosting service carries an operated service's duties: uploader identity, private assets that stay private and public delivery only by explicit choice (INT-79), upload credentials kept out of source and agent context (ARC-23), abuse and takedown handling, and privacy terms that name its operator (FEA-SF-32, INT-73).

Open: each server's identity source and role mapping (FEA-SF-19, FEA-BR-25); for the hosting service, how uploaders identify themselves (an account, an API key or a sign-in), pricing (free, limited or paid; INT-30), quotas for storage, file size and delivery, the provider (INT-48), retention and deletion when an uploader leaves, and abuse handling.

items.question: Which sharing paths does RichView offer, and which services does RichView itself operate?
items.why: The CLI and VS Code still publish to `https://richview.uk` by default, the home page promises private reports and access control, and the server protects only writes; the answer fixes the sharing model and these claims.
items.proposed: Stories are shared three ways: the self-contained HTML file, a PDF, and a self-hostable RichView server. RichView Cowork (INT-83), today's report host renamed, shares inside an organisation: it stores immutable, permanent versions at stable URLs (`/r/:slug`, `/r/:slug/v/:version`; ARC-21, TYP-63, TYP-64), delivers each report as a small page that links the report runtime and fonts from content-hashed, immutably cached routes on the same host, and offers the self-contained file as a download (INT-04, ARC-24, FEA-SF-20). RichView Publish (INT-35) shares outward as an editorial publication. In the first cut Cowork requires a token for publish, render and regenerate, except renders on the loopback preview (ARC-31), and reads are open to anyone who can reach it; its target, as for every RichView server, is a basic role set of reader, author and owner, with rights to edit, delete and share, while the core keeps no accounts (INT-27, FEA-SF-19). RichView runs no Cowork or Publish server for others: the one service it operates is managed hosting for large data and media that reports reference (INT-27, TYP-41), and the one Publish instance it runs is its own News (INT-74). The CLI and VS Code have no default server; publishing names one explicitly (TYP-67, FEA-SF-12). Private reads and a report menu are D-ACCESS-CLAIM’s (FEA-SF-19), and public copy claims only what exists.

sources.label: Daniel's INT-43 answer: launch happens when Daniel says so, and everything goes live at once (site, try path, flagship, docs, public source); no date, nothing else gates it, and no wedge naming is required; first posts only after his review

Daniel's INT-36 answer: hosted Cowork at app.richview.ai, free up to limits and paid beyond them; Publish servers run for customers under their own DNS; paid services are the business model; pricing, limits and hosted-only features open

Daniel's INT-31 answer: the rewrite builds the core plus RichView Cowork and Publish (News is a Publish instance), scrollytelling, uploads and a managed hosting service; the LinkedIn carousel is dropped
D9 “The one signal that users love it?”: “Agents reach ‘verified clean’ unattended AND a human keeps the report”; “Installs/stars are lagging vanity proxies.”
Goal: “Generate interest and collect feedback from analysts and developers using coding agents”
Site brief: “Generate interest and useful feedback with work people can inspect”
“Define the launch wedge: first users, first artifact they publish, and the loop that brings them back.”

items.conflicts: The 2026-10-02 goal was interest and feedback, not kept reports. Until the source is public and the list may be emailed (INT-72), RichView has no channel for outside feedback. Before launch, Daniel’s INT-21 answer has scored fresh-agent runs measure the agent half of this signal without telemetry (FEA-SF-65).
